explanation: Its wings swivel at the shoulder and push air on both the forward and the back stroke, so it can hover at a flower and reverse away from it.

claims.text: Swifts, kingfishers and swallows cannot fly backwards.
A hummingbird's wings rotate at the shoulder joint and produce lift on both the downstroke and the upstroke.
This wing action lets hummingbirds hover at flowers and fly in reverse.

evidence.restatement: Hummingbirds can hover and fly backwards.
Swifts, swallows and kingfishers fly forwards; a hovering kingfisher holds position but does not fly in reverse. Hummingbirds are the only birds known for sustained backward flight.
A hummingbird's wing rotates at the shoulder, so it makes lift on the upstroke as well as the downstroke.
That stroke lets hummingbirds hover in front of flowers and back away from them.
Hummingbirds can fly backwards, and they are the one bird group known for doing it under their own power.
Swifts and swallows fly forwards only; kingfishers can hover but do not reverse under their own power.

claimResults.note: One search (low-tier pages only) says other birds can shuffle backwards for a few wingbeats, usually with wind help, and that kingfishers and swallows hover by facing the wind. Nothing reports sustained backward flight for these three. I read "cannot fly backwards" as "no sustained backward flight".
